title: The Forest Insect and Disturbance Lab
text:
Welcome to the Forest Insect and Disturbance Lab at Utah State University! Our research is focused on how weather, climate, and landscapes affect forest insect herbivores, disturbances, and forest ecosystems. We are especially interested in identifying the mechanisms of  where, when, and how population irruptions by native forest insect herbivores start to better forecast future outbreaks.



Research Themes

exploring the mechanisms of insect population irruptions at local and landscape scales
quantifying and identifying native and invasive threats to healthy forests in Utah and beyond
modeling the consequences of insect-caused disturbance and climate change across forested ecosystems
exploring forest dynamics in a changing world
expanding our toolbox for explaining and forecasting climate change impacts across ecosystems and continents

title: Research
text:
Population irruptions (i.e., outbreaks) by native forest insect herbivores are a leading cause of disturbance across forested landscapes. The extent and severity of these outbreaks, whether caused by sawflies, caterpillars, or bark beetles, are affected by both the long-term effects of climate and the short-term effects of fluctuating weather. As a result, outbreaks by forest are highly sensitive to climatic change.

title: Modeling w/Mike
text:
Howe and Nelson in prep.

Please cite this manuscript if you use our generic code examples.
Code Block 1: Generic example of model construction using A) S3 objects (mlr) and B) R6 objects (mlr3). In both approaches we are randomly drawing a training (train.set) and test (test.set) dataset from our full dataset (full.dataset). The model stacking ensemble that we use in B requires mlr3pipelines.
1.A

#### S3: mlr  ####

learner.randomforest = setHyperPars(
              makeLearner("classif.ranger", 
              num.threads=12, 
              predict.type = "prob", 
              importance="impurity", 
              predict.threshold = 0.5), 
              par.vals = list(num.trees=250, verbose=TRUE))

learner.XGBoost = setHyperPars(
              makeLearner("classif.xgboost", 
              nthread=12, 
              predict.type = "prob", 
              predict.threshold = 0.5), 
              par.vals = list(nrounds = 250,
              max_depth = 8,
              alpha=0.022,
              eta = 0.36, 
              lambda = 0.1))

ensemble = makeStackedLearner(base.learners = list(
    learner.randomforest, 
    learner.XGBoost),
    method="average",
    predict.type = "prob")

train.set <- full.dataset %>%
    group_by(mpb) %>%
    slice_sample(n=50000) %>%
    mutate(mpb=as.factor(mpb)) %>%
    as.data.frame()
  
test.set <- full.dataset %>%
    group_by(mpb) %>%
    slice_sample(n=50000) %>%
    mutate(mpb=as.factor(mpb)) %>%
    as.data.frame()
  
model.train <- train.set %>%
    makeClassifTask(data=., target="mpb", positive="1") %>%
    train(ensemble, .)

model.predict <- test.set %>%
    makeClassifTask(data=., target="mpb", positive="1") %>%
    predict(model.train, .)

1.B

#### R6: mlr3 ####

learner.randomforest <- lrn(
  "classif.ranger", 
  num.threads=12, 
  num.trees = 250, 
  importance="impurity",
  predict_type="prob")

learner.XGBoost <- lrn(
  "classif.xgboost",
  nthread=12,
  alpha=0.022,
  eta = 0.36, 
  lambda = 0.1,
  max_depth=8,
  nrounds=250,
  predict_type="prob")

train.set <- full.dataset %>%
    group_by(mpb) %>%
    slice_sample(n=50000) %>%
    as.data.frame()
  
test.set <- full.dataset %>%
    group_by(mpb) %>%
    slice_sample(n=50000) %>%
    as.data.frame()

training.task <- as_task_classif(x=train.set, target="mpb")  
testing.task <-  as_task_classif(x=test.set, target="mpb")  

ensemble.pipeline <- 
  gunion(list(
    PipeOpLearnerCV$new(learner.randomforest, id = "xgb"),
    PipeOpLearnerCV$new(learner.XGBoost, id = "rf")
  ))

ensemble.average <- LearnerClassifAvg$new(id = "classif")

ensemble.model <- ensemble.pipeline %>>%
  PipeOpFeatureUnion$new(2, id = "avg") %>>%
  ensemble.average

ensemble <- GraphLearner$new(ensemble.model, predict_type="prob")
model.train <- ensemble$train(training.task)
model.test <- ensemble$predict(test.task)

Code Block 2: Generic example of hyperparameter tuning using the default tuning space for XGBoost. We constrained the number of rounds to 250-500 and the max depth to 5-10 based on processing limitations.

#### tuning space ###

xgboost.lts <- lts("classif.xgboost.default",
              nrounds=to_tune(250, 500),
              max_depth=to_tune(5,10),
              subsample=NULL,
              colsample_bylevel=NULL,
              colsample_bytree=NULL)

#### tuner ####

xgboost.ti <- ti(
  task=training.task,
  learner=lrn("classif.xgboost", nthread=12),
  resampling=rsmp("cv", folds=3),
  measures = msr("classif.ce"),
  terminator=trm("evals", n_evals=10),
  search_space = c.xgb.lts
)

#### grid search  ####

xgboost.tnr <- tnr("grid_search", batch_size=50)

#### optimize ####

xgboost.tnr$optimize(xgboost.ti)

Code Block 3: Generic example of forward selection using A) mlr3fselect; and B) our forward selection algorithm. Our variable selection function ‘var.selex’ calls the function ‘ensemble.model’ which simply takes a list of training and testing datasets (one for each predictor), fits a model based on the training dataset and calculates perforamnce based on the testing dataset.
3.A

model.fselect = fselect(
  fselector = fs("sequential", max_features=10),
  task = training.task,
  learner = ensemble,
  resampling = rsmp("holdout"),
  measure = msr("classif.ce"))

3.B

ensemble.model <- function(df.train, df.test){
  
  df.prdctr <- df.train %>% select(predictor) %>% distinct() %>% pull()
  df.trn <- df.train %>% select(-predictor)
  df.tst <- df.test %>% select(-predictor)
  
  sample.tsk <- as_task_classif(x=df.trn, target="mpb")
  sample.tst <- as_task_classif(x=df.tst, target="mpb")

  m.e.cv = GraphLearner$new(m.1, predict_type="prob")  
  m.train <- m.e.cv$train(sample.tsk)
  m.prd <- m.e.cv$predict(sample.tst)
  
  m.prf <- data.frame(
    acc = m.prd$score(msr("classif.acc")),
    auc = m.prd$score(msr("classif.auc")),
    ce = m.prd$score(msr("classif.ce")),
    fdr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fdr")),
    fnr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fnr")),
    fomr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fomr")),
    fpr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fpr")),
    tnr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.tnr")),
    tpr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.tpr"))) %>%
    as_tibble() %>% bind_cols(t(m.train$timings) %>% as_tibble()) %>% 
    mutate(predictor=df.prdctr)

  return(m.prf)
  
}

`%ni%` <- Negate(`%in%`)

var.selex <- function(train.df, test.df, max.feat=14, cutoff=0.8, iter=j){
  
  #### correlation matrix ####
  
  corr.mat <- bind_rows(
    train.df %>% 
    bind_rows(test.df) %>%
    select(-mpb) %>% 
    as.matrix() %>% 
    cor(., method="pearson") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column() %>%
    pivot_longer(-rowname) %>%
    mutate(method="pearson"),
    train.df %>% 
    bind_rows(test.df) %>%
    select(-mpb) %>% 
    as.matrix() %>% 
    cor(., method="spearman") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column() %>%
    pivot_longer(-rowname) %>%
    mutate(method="spearman")) %>%
    mutate(abs.value=abs(value)) %>%
    select(var.1=rowname,
           var.2=name,
           method, abs.value) %>%
    pivot_wider(values_from=abs.value, names_from=method)
  
  #### result.grid  ####
  
  result.grid <- list()

  for(i in 1:max.feat){
    
  print(paste0("#### model ", i, " ####"))  
    
  if(i == 1){  

  train.split <- train.df %>%
  pivot_longer(-mpb, names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
  split(.$predictor, drop=TRUE) 
  
  test.split <- test.df %>%
  pivot_longer(-mpb, names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
  split(.$predictor)    
  
  model <- map2(.x=train.split, .y=test.split, .f=ensemble.model) %>% bind_rows()  
  
result.grid[[i]] <- p.s <- model %>% mutate(n.feat=i)
   
  }else{
    
  p.s <- result.grid %>% bind_rows() %>% group_by(n.feat) %>%
    slice_min(order_by=ce) %>% ungroup()
  
  crm <- corr.mat %>%
    filter(var.1 %in% p.s$predictor) %>%
    filter(pearson >= cutoff | spearman >= cutoff)
  
  can.var <- corr.mat %>% filter(var.2 %ni% crm$var.2) %>%
    select(var.2) %>% distinct()
    
  if(nrow(can.var) > 0){
  
  train.split <- train.df %>%
    select(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor), contains(can.var$var.2)) %>%
    pivot_longer(!c(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor)), names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
    split(.$predictor, drop=TRUE) 
  
  test.split <- test.df %>%
    select(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor), contains(can.var$var.2)) %>%
    pivot_longer(!c(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor)), names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
    split(.$predictor, drop=TRUE) 
  
  model <- map2(.x=train.split, .y=test.split, .f=ensemble.model) %>% bind_rows()
  
  result.grid[[i]] <- p.s <- model %>% mutate(n.feat=i)
  }
  
  print("done")
  
  }  
    
    
  }
  
  results <- result.grid %>% bind_rows() %>%
    write_csv(paste0("var.selex/vs.", iter, ".csv"))
  
}

Code Block 4: Methods and code for model interpretation.

#### explain_mlr3 allows us to easily interpret mlr3 based models

mpb.exp <- explain_mlr3(model=ensemble,
                        data=test.set %>% select(-mpb),
                           y=test.set %>% select(mpb)) 

#### model_profile allows us to create accumulated local dependence profiles; 'variable_splits_with_obs=TRUE' is an additional useful option as it predicts all existing unique values in the test data set (do not use if values are not rounded).

mpb.mp <- model_profile(mpb.exp, type="accumulated", N=1000, variable_splits_with_obs=TRUE)

#### relativizing profiles by mean predictions (relative mean predictions)
mean.exp <- mean(mpb.exp$y_hat)

x.mt <- mpb.mp$agr_profiles %>%
    janitor::clean_names() %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(y0=mean.exp) %>%
    select(variable=vname, x=x, yhat=yhat, y0) %>%
    mutate(yt=yhat-y0, iter=iter) 

#### model performance based on:

#### the model explainer
model.performance <- model_performance(mpb.exp)
  
#### directly from mlr3
model.performance <- data.frame(
    acc = model.test$score(msr("classif.acc")),
    auc = model.test$score(msr("classif.auc")),
    ce = model.test$score(msr("classif.ce")),
    fdr = model.test$score(msr("classif.fdr")),
    fnr = model.test$score(msr("classif.fnr")),
    fomr = model.test$score(msr("classif.fomr")),
    fpr = model.test$score(msr("classif.fpr")),
    tnr = model.test$score(msr("classif.tnr")),
    tpr = model.test$score(msr("classif.tpr"))) %>%
  mutate(iter=iter)

#### variable importance

variable.importance <- bind_rows(
    model_parts(mpb.exp) %>% as.data.frame())
  
#### interactions (h2)
friedmans.h2 <- hstats::hstats(mpb.exp)
summary.h2 <- summary(friedmans.h2)

two.way <- summary.h2$h2_pairwise$M %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column() %>%
    select(inx=rowname, h2=V1) %>%
    mutate(type="two-way")
    
one.way <- summary.h2$h2_overall$M %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column() %>%
    select(inx=rowname, h2=V1) %>%
    mutate(type="one-way") 
  
overall <- data.frame(inx="overall", h2=summary.h2$h2$M, type="overall")

    auc = m.prd$score(msr("classif.auc")),
    ce = m.prd$score(msr("classif.ce")),
    fdr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fdr")),
    fnr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fnr")),
    fomr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fomr")),
    fpr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.fpr")),
    tnr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.tnr")),
    tpr = m.prd$score(msr("classif.tpr"))) %>%
    as_tibble() %>% bind_cols(t(m.train$timings) %>% as_tibble()) %>% 
    mutate(predictor=df.prdctr)

  return(m.prf)
  
}

`%ni%` <- Negate(`%in%`)

var.selex <- function(train.df, test.df, max.feat=14, cutoff=0.8, iter=j){
  
  #### correlation matrix ####
  # NOTE: this is messy and I'll rewrite it at some point
  
  corr.mat <- bind_rows(
    train.df %>% 
    bind_rows(test.df) %>%
    select(-mpb) %>% 
    as.matrix() %>% 
    cor(., method="pearson") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column() %>%
    pivot_longer(-rowname) %>%
    mutate(method="pearson"),
    train.df %>% 
    bind_rows(test.df) %>%
    select(-mpb) %>% 
    as.matrix() %>% 
    cor(., method="spearman") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column() %>%
    pivot_longer(-rowname) %>%
    mutate(method="spearman")) %>%
    mutate(abs.value=abs(value)) %>%
    select(var.1=rowname,
           var.2=name,
           method, abs.value) %>%
    pivot_wider(values_from=abs.value, names_from=method)
  
  #### result.grid  ####
  
  result.grid <- list()

  for(i in 1:max.feat){
    
  print(paste0("#### model ", i, " ####"))  
    
  if(i == 1){  

  train.split <- train.df %>%
  pivot_longer(-mpb, names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
  split(.$predictor, drop=TRUE) 
  
  test.split <- test.df %>%
  pivot_longer(-mpb, names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
  split(.$predictor)    
  
  model <- map2(.x=train.split, .y=test.split, .f=ensemble.model) %>% bind_rows()  
  
result.grid[[i]] <- p.s <- model %>% mutate(n.feat=i)
   
  }else{
    
  p.s <- result.grid %>% bind_rows() %>% group_by(n.feat) %>%
    slice_min(order_by=ce) %>% ungroup()
  
  crm <- corr.mat %>%
    filter(var.1 %in% p.s$predictor) %>%
    filter(pearson >= cutoff | spearman >= cutoff)
  
  can.var <- corr.mat %>% filter(var.2 %ni% crm$var.2) %>%
    select(var.2) %>% distinct()
    
  if(nrow(can.var) > 0){
  
  train.split <- train.df %>%
    select(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor), contains(can.var$var.2)) %>%
    pivot_longer(!c(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor)), names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
    split(.$predictor, drop=TRUE) 
  
  test.split <- test.df %>%
    select(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor), contains(can.var$var.2)) %>%
    pivot_longer(!c(mpb, contains(p.s$predictor)), names_to="predictor", values_to="obs") %>%
    split(.$predictor, drop=TRUE) 
  
  model <- map2(.x=train.split, .y=test.split, .f=ensemble.model) %>% bind_rows()
  
  result.grid[[i]] <- p.s <- model %>% mutate(n.feat=i)
  }
  
  print("done")
  
  }  
    
    
  }
  
  results <- result.grid %>% bind_rows() %>%
    write_csv(paste0("var.selex/vs.", iter, ".csv"))
  
}

I am an ecologist and entomologist interested in how insects respond to changes in their landscape. I have worn a bunch of hats in my research career, working on topics ranging from insect foraging behavior to continental-scale analyses of shifts in community composition. I’m just as excited about big, creative experiments as I am about using existing data and some R sorcery to uncover cool new patterns. My work has largely used bumble bees as a model system, and a lot of my work still focuses on bumble and other wild bees. I have a special interest for understanding, promoting, and managing insects in agricultural landscapes.
Outside of work, I’m keen to stay active and enjoy playing hockey, running, riding all of the bikes, and have been climbing for almost 20 years. I have a daughter named Fiadh (“Fee-ah”), a wife named Megan, and a menagerie of animals including two dogs, two cats, and 6 chickens. When I’m not doing all of this, you’ll usually find me in the kitchen slingin’ bread dough and cooking (mostly) tasty food.
